back: The population is the whole group of interest; a sample is the part of it that is actually studied.
A numbered list of the members of the population from which the sample is chosen.
A census is complete but slow and costly; a sample is quicker and cheaper and is essential when testing destroys items.
Every possible sample of the required size is equally likely; use lots or random numbers on a numbered frame.
$k = \dfrac{\text{population size}}{\text{sample size}}$; random start from 1 to $k$, then every $k$th member.
Whole natural groups (villages, schools) are chosen at random and studied.
Non-random: quota fills set numbers per group by the interviewer's choice; convenience takes whoever is easiest to reach.
A method is biased if it systematically over- or under-represents some groups; a bigger biased sample is still biased.
